interventions.description: Synthetic fairness report discussing the fictional prosecution.
A later synthetic comment. It is dated after the conviction and is not treated as explaining that conviction.

arguments.summary: The report argues that the restriction is disproportionate because a two-year prison sentence was sought for one satirical post.
arguments.reasons: The fictional report compares imprisonment with the stated aim of protecting public order and notes that a correction or a civil remedy was not addressed.
arguments.passage: The report argues that the restriction is disproportionate because a two-year prison sentence for a single satirical post goes beyond the stated aim, and the court was not shown to have considered a correction or a civil remedy.
arguments.legal_authorities: Mentioned in the synthetic report only: Exampleland Constitution art. 19; ICCPR art. 19(3).

arguments.summary: The report argues that a ban on future posts about the same official is a disproportionate prior restraint.
arguments.reasons: The fictional report says the order covers speech that has not been made and is not tied to a specific threat.
arguments.passage: The report argues that forbidding any future post about the official is disproportionate because it restrains speech that has not occurred and is not linked to a defined risk.
arguments.legal_authorities: Mentioned in the synthetic report only: ICCPR art. 19(3).

arguments.summary: The report argues that the offense is vague because it turns on speech 'harmful to public calm' without defining that phrase.
arguments.reasons: The fictional report says the phrase gives officials open-ended discretion.
arguments.passage: The report argues that the offense is vague because 'harmful to public calm' is undefined and leaves officials to decide which criticism is criminal.
arguments.legal_authorities: Mentioned in the synthetic report only: Exampleland Criminal Code s. 4.

arguments.summary: The report describes counsel's argument that the charge sheet was filed out of time. That is counsel's argument, not TrialWatch's reasoning.
arguments.reasons: The fictional report attributes the filing-deadline point to counsel and does not adopt it as the report's own argument.
arguments.passage: Counsel submitted that the charge sheet was filed out of time.

arguments.summary: A model suggested a further proportionality point, but no passage was captured.

outcomes.description: The fictional trial court convicted A. Rivera and imposed two years' imprisonment.
